title: Thanks for the Letter and Its Question
english: Letter 80. To Bishop Optimus. On the words, “Whoever kills Cain will be punished sevenfold” (Genesis 4:15).

In any case I am glad to see these good boys, both for the steadiness of character that is beyond their years and for their close tie to Your Reverence, from which one may expect something great of them. When I saw them coming to me with a letter of yours, I doubled my affection for them. And when I read the letter and saw in it both your provident care for the churches and your diligence in reading the divine Scriptures, I gave thanks to the Lord, and I prayed for blessings on those who brought us such a letter, and before them on the one who wrote it to us.

You asked about that much-discussed saying, repeated everywhere by everyone: what is the solution to “Whoever kills Cain will release seven punishments” (Genesis 4:15)? In this, first of all, you have commended yourself as one who carefully keeps the charge to Timothy, just as Paul gave it to him; for you are plainly attending to reading (1 Timothy 4:13).
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 77, cols. 365-368, Letter 80 (Ad Optimum episcopum).
Author: this letter is Basil of Caesarea's Letter 260, to Bishop Optimus. PG 77 prints it among the letters of Cyril of Alexandria as Letter 80.

The first paragraph renders the Latin editorial heading of PG, not the author's Greek. The heading follows the Vulgate ('will be punished sevenfold'); the letter quotes the Septuagint, where παραλύσει ('will release, undo') and ἐκδικούμενα ('things avenged, punishments') carry the sense the letter goes on to explain. 'Release seven punishments' keeps that wording so the later argument reads straight.
τὸ πρὸς τὴν σὴν εὐλάβειαν οἰκεῖον: 'their close tie to Your Reverence'; οἰκεῖον may mean kinship or closeness of household, and the Greek does not say which.
τέως μέν is answered by Ἔπειτα καί at the start of the next section ('first of all ... then, too').
